extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of sociology, political science, and criminology (especially those studying state power, moral panics, and 1970s Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the conditions, discourses, and institutional shifts by which social 'crises' (crime, terrorism, industrial unrest) are signified and managed by the state, media, and judiciary, using the 1970–1972 British case as exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory mobilisation and 'preparedness' in control apparatuses
rubrics_metrics.description: A state of anticipatory mobilisation and 'preparedness' in the control apparatuses is an essential pre-condition for the development of a panic or exceptional posture by the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of five essential conditions for the 'mugging panic' — implies that police, courts and other control agencies must be organised and ready to act for a panic to be manufactured or sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitising of official circles and the public through the mass media
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensitising of official circles and of the public through the mass media is required to create receptive opinion for crisis narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media amplification is a distinct condition: press and television portrayals make official circles and the public expect and fear disorder, enabling recruitment to law-and-order solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Perceived danger' to social stability (crime rate as index)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'perceived danger' to social stability — for example when the crime rate is read as indexing a general breakdown in social authority and control — helps trigger a crisis reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The perception (not necessarily objective reality) that social order is threatened legitimates exceptional responses; evaluation must pay attention to how statistics and narratives are interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of a vulnerable 'target group' in dramatic incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of a vulnerable 'target group' (e.g. black youth) involved in dramatic incidents ('muggings') which trigger public alarm is a necessary element in producing a moral panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scapegoating or focusing public fear onto a particular social group helps convert isolated incidents into a generalised threat; look for repeated emphasis on group identity in coverage and official statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms projecting conspiratorial demons and criminal folk-devils
rubrics_metrics.description: The setting in motion of mechanisms by which conspiratorial demons and criminal folk-devils are projected onto the public stage transforms discrete problems into symbolic threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes discursive moves, symbolic exemplars, and institutional interventions that construct and circulate a villainous figure to embody the crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence as the axis/ultimate threshold in signifying crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Violence is the axis around which the public signification of the crisis turns in 1972: 'violence' functions as the ultimate threshold, the lowest common denominator that converts many threats into 'the threat'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should trace how disparate conflicts are collapsed into the abstract category 'violence' (often defined as anarchic, irrational, or 'pointless'), thereby simplifying public meaning and enabling hardline responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary framing: law presented as the opposite/answer to violence
rubrics_metrics.description: The binary opposite of violence is repeatedly signified as 'the law' — editorials argue that only law, 'fairly and legally administered', can guarantee peace and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should note how appeals to the law are used rhetorically to delegitimate dissent and to justify legal/penal measures; even 'bad laws' are framed as preferable to 'the rule of force'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment of the law to win public consent for a stronger state
rubrics_metrics.description: The active recruitment of 'the law' in defence of class interests and in public discourse serves to make authoritarian or repressive measures more legitimate to the 'silent majority'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for examples where law/courts are openly marshalled to defend particular political outcomes and how this mobilises popular opinion in favour of a 'strong state'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of the law and courts into political management of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension of the law and the courts into the political management of conflict and class struggle (i.e. using juridical instruments to regulate industrial relations and dissent) is a central feature of the period's state reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how legal mechanisms (e.g., outlawing tactics, conspiracy charges, industrial-relations legislation) are deployed as instruments of political control, not merely neutral dispute resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction of the capitalist state via progressive intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: The capitalist state is being reconstructed by progressive intervention into areas formerly belonging to 'civil society' — the economy, ideological relations, and social reproduction — altering the state's role and capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating state change, account for interventions across economic management, welfare/domestic reproduction, and ideological apparatuses; consider whether shifts are national or shareable across advanced capitalist states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation of law risks exposing judicial impartiality and social inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking the law in open defence of class interests risks making previously 'invisible' inequalities and the partiality of juridical institutions manifest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should examine whether legal intervention strips the judiciary of perceived neutrality and how that affects the legitimacy of state actions and class consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media simplification: dissolving political context into abstract violence and innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: Media narratives often practice simplification by dissolving concrete political conflicts into abstract categories of 'violence' and 'innocent victims', thereby erasing political and historical contextualisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should track how reportage abstracts individual events into universalized 'Everyman' victims and neglects structural causes (e.g., imperialism, exploitation), which facilitates depoliticised moral outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and juridical escalation as response to industrial resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern where industrial resistance (e.g., miners' tactics, flying pickets) is met by successive legal constraints (e.g., outlawing flying pickets, conspiracy charges) representing a juridical escalation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sequences of legal measures as strategic state responses designed to criminalise specific forms of collective action rather than neutral regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media portrayal of terrorism as 'senseless' amplifies fear and decontextualises causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The repeated view that terrorism is 'senseless' and the product of collective irrationality helps to signify crises as beyond comprehension and ramps up public fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should identify depictions that frame political violence as irrational and disconnected from political causes, and note how such framing supports emergency legislation and public alarm.
